extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians, teachers, and advanced students interested in classical analytic geometry, trigonometry, and problem solutions
extracted.subtask_short: solving advanced geometry and trig problems
extracted.subtask_description: Classical analytic-geometry and trigonometry problem statements, worked examples, and solution methods (locus problems for quadrics, trig table/antitangent computation, descriptive-geometry constructions, magnetometer/astronomical formula derivations). Intended for readers reproducing or understanding these solutions and computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute tangent via complementary angle when convenient
rubrics_metrics.description: When computing tan of an angle, reduce by complement if appropriate (e.g. to find tan 67°30' first find tan(90°—67°30') = tan 22°30').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The worked example (Example II) explicitly uses art. 10: find tan(90°— angle) and then proceed with table lookups and stepwise multiplications/subtractions as shown in the numeric computation. Follow the sequence of table-derived multipliers and corrections (including small-term corrections) as demonstrated in the example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain inverse sines/cosines/etc. via tangent-based methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The values of sin^-1, cos^-1, sec^-1, cosec^-1 and of sin a, cos a, sec a, cosec a may be found by the methods developed for tangents, though with generally greater labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For instance, to calculate sin^-1(a) compute its equivalent expression involving tangents; having found tan a (by arts. 8, 10), use algebraic relations (e.g. sina = ... or formulas involving sqrt expressions) to recover sine/cosine. Expect heavier algebraic work and nested radical evaluations compared to tan computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use polar/quadratic roots to express chord/segment ratio and deduce locus (surface of second degree)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line from point P to fixed point A meets a given surface of second degree in Q and Q', and p and p' are roots of the polar equation, then substituting quadratic relations for p and p' into the ratio PQ×PQ' : AQ×AQ' yields an expression which shows the locus of P is a surface of the second degree similar and concentric to the given one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up the polar equation of the surface (denoted briefly Mp+Nv+1=0). Use quadratic relations (p+p' = M, 1+pp' = -N) to substitute into the ratio expression. The algebraic manipulation demonstrates the locus is a quadric; follow the pattern shown in Article XIX for analogous problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate perpendicular-distance geometric relations into algebraic equations using formulae (1),(2),(2')
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpendiculars from a point to a plane or surface can be expressed algebraically: e.g., given plane equation αx+βy+γz+1=0 and coordinates of P, the perpendicular PM relates via PM^2 = αx'+βy'+γz'+1 (equation (2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equations (1),(2),(2') are essential for converting geometric statements about perpendiculars and ratios of segments into algebraic relations. Use these equations to form ratios (e.g., PM : AN :: PQ : AQ) and manipulate them to obtain loci equations (see Articles XX–XXVIII).

rubrics_metrics.name: General method for locus problems with given ratios of products of perpendiculars
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the locus of P such that products/ratios of perpendiculars (e.g., PM'×PM* : PMi×PMj or PQ×PQ' : PR×PR') have given proportional relationships, set up the plane/surface equations with coordinates through a fixed point A, express perpendiculars via the algebraic relations, and reduce to an equation of the form u = m v (or similar), which denotes a system/surface of second degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The articles (XXI–XXVIII) follow a repeated template: (1) express given planes/surfaces as equations referenced to axes through A; (2) let u, v denote the algebraic forms given by equation (2); (3) impose the required ratio (u = m v, u = m v^2, etc.); (4) deduce the locus properties — e.g., passes through intersections, touches a surface along a curve, is a family of similar quadrics, yields involution relations among intersection points. Reproduce these algebraic substitutions and consequent geometric conclusions as in the examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive astronomical equal-altitude formula by small-angle and algebraic elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: For the formula computing the equation of equal altitudes, treat C and E as small and approximate by their sines; introduce P (polar distance at noon), C (change of declination), I (elapsed time), and E (equation of equal altitudes), then manipulate trig identities, subtract and divide relations, and eliminate to obtain E in terms of C, P, I, latitude (L).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the stepwise derivation: use trig identities to express combinations like cos(P+I)sin(C−E)+cos(P−I)sin(C+E), equate to expressions from differences of sines, divide and simplify, then isolate E. For numerical use, map the algebraic result to table/logarithm computations as shown (Log A = log(...), etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statics-based derivation for vertical-force magnetometer equilibria
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the magnetic needle with vertical and horizontal components F=M sin φ and H=M cos φ; use the statical equation of virtual velocities F ż + H ẏ = 0, substitute particle contributions (e.g., ż = a cos cos I, ẏ = a sin φ), and derive equilibrium relations (cot φ = cot δ cos I) and force expressions F = M cos φ tan cos I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive alternative equivalent forms (e.g., Biot's formula) by manipulating trig identities and perform logarithmic differentiation to obtain sensitivity relations for small deviations. For counterpoised needles include constant moment μ and substitute F−μ. Use vibration time comparisons to estimate small angular deviations experimentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct shadows and perspectives in descriptive geometry via two lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Given projections of two points of a line and traces of a plane, use Lemma 1 (construct traces of a line from its point projections) and Lemma 2 (given two point projections and plane traces, construct projections of line–plane intersection) to find the shadow projections and then the perspective from an eye point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: find intersection of ray from luminous point A with the plane (use Lemma 2) to obtain shadow endpoints' projections on horizontal and vertical planes; then to obtain perspective from the eye, draw lines from shadow endpoints to the eye and find where they pierce the picture plane (use Lemma 1). Follow the short worked example (Putney College Examination) for mapping between horizontal/vertical projections and picture-plane traces.
